concerns.text: FR-007 and Edge Cases define 'unphysical' trajectories as those leaving the attractor for sigma > 0.1 and mandate halting analysis. This creates a circular validation: the study aims to quantify noise-induced bias in FTLE, but the validation protocol explicitly excludes the very high-noise regime where the bias is expected to be maximal and non-linear. By conditioning the analysis on 'bounded trajectories only' without modeling the escape probability, the spec introduces survivorship bias that invalidates the claimed scaling laws for the full noise range.

The spec defines the 'asymptotic baseline' (ground truth) as the numerically computed limit of the *clean* system (US-2, FR-003). However, the research question asks how FTLE deviates in *noisy* systems. In chaotic systems with observational noise, the 'true' finite-time exponent is a stochastic variable whose expectation value differs from the clean asymptotic limit. Using the clean limit as the sole ground truth for noisy trajectories conflates 'finite-time convergence error' with 'noise-induced bias'. The validation target (clean limit) is definitionally independent of the noise predictor, but the *interpretation* of the deviation as purely 'noise-induced' is scientifically unsound without separating the finite-time convergence component from the noise component.

US-3 and FR-004 mandate a t-test and regression for deviation scaling. The spec fails to specify the statistical model for the noise-induced bias. In chaotic systems, FTLE estimates are not independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) across time windows due to trajectory correlation. A standard t-test or OLS regression without accounting for autocorrelation in the residuals or the specific distribution of Lyapunov exponents (often non-Gaussian) will yield invalid p-values and confidence intervals. The methodology assumes standard statistical properties that do not hold for chaotic time-series data.
